entry:
Totality of psychological phenomena and capacities, encompassing both conscious and unconscious states. The mind is that which thinks, feels, perceives, imagines, remembers, and wills. Conscious processes make an individual aware of external and internal circumstances; unconscious processes can influence an individual without intention or awareness. Its exact nature is disputed: some characterizations stress internal aspects, saying that the mind transforms information and is not directly accessible to outside observers, while others understand mental phenomena as dispositions to engage in observable behavior. In a narrow sense the term covers only cognitive functions associated with perception, reasoning, awareness, and memory; in a broader sense it also includes feeling, motivation, and behavior.

The English word derives from [[Old English]] *gemynd*, meaning "memory", which gave rise to [[Middle English]] forms and slowly expanded to cover all mental capacities. Cognates include the ancient Greek μένος, the [[Latin]] *mens*, and the Sanskrit *manas*. Psyche and mentality are usually treated as synonyms, while soul, spirit, cognition, intellect, intelligence, and brain overlap with mind without meaning exactly the same. The brain is the physical organ responsible for most or all mental functions.

The mind encompasses [[Perception|perception]], [[Memory|memory]], thought, [[Imagination|imagination]], motivation, emotion, attention, learning, and consciousness. Perception interprets and organizes sensory information from the sense organs and is shaped by past experiences, cultural background, beliefs, knowledge, and expectations. Memory stores and retrieves information. Episodic memory concerns specific past events, semantic memory general knowledge, and procedural memory how to do things; short-term memory holds information for brief periods, while long-term memory can last a lifetime. Thinking is goal-oriented processing of information and manipulation of concepts, and includes logical reasoning, problem-solving, and decision-making; some theorists hold that all thought happens through language. Imagination internally generates mental images and ideas without direct stimulation of the sense organs, and plays a key role in art and literature.

The mind–body problem is the challenge of explaining the relation between matter and mind. Traditionally the two were often thought of as distinct substances that could exist independently; René Descartes's 17th-century dualism conceived the mind as a non-spatial, spiritual substance interacting with the body through the pineal gland. The dominant philosophical position since the 20th century has been physicalism, which holds that everything is material, so that minds are aspects or features of certain material objects. The evolutionary history of the mind is tied to the development of nervous systems and brains: as brains became more complex, mental functions grew in number and capacity, with particular brain areas dedicated to specific functions. Individual minds develop as people learn from experience and pass through psychological stages in the process of aging. Some people are affected by [[Mental disorder|mental disorders]], in which certain mental capacities do not function as they should. It is widely accepted that at least some non-human animals have some form of mind, but which animals is controversial. Theorists also discuss the possibility and consequences of creating artificial minds with computers.

The main fields studying the mind are psychology, neuroscience, cognitive science, and [[Philosophy of mind|philosophy of mind]]. They focus on different aspects and use different methods, from empirical observation and neuroimaging to conceptual analysis and thought experiments.

Naturally occurring solid with a fairly well-defined chemical composition and a specific crystal structure. The geological definition normally excludes compounds that occur only in living organisms, though some minerals, such as calcite, are often biogenic. A mineral is distinct from a [[Rock (geology)|rock]], which is bulk solid geologic material that may consist of one mineral or an aggregate of several.

The International Mineralogical Association (IMA), the standard body for defining and naming mineral species, recognizes 6,228 species. It requires that a mineral be naturally occurring, formed by geological processes, solid in its natural occurrence, and have a well-defined crystallographic structure and a fairly well-defined composition. Substances generated only by human activity or in living beings, such as tungsten carbide and seashells, are excluded, but taranakite, derived from bat guano, qualifies because geological processes were involved. Native [[Mercury (element)|mercury]] is classified as a mineral, though it crystallizes only below −39 °C, because it was included before the current rules. Water [[Ice|ice]] is a mineral; liquid water and carbon dioxide are not. Amorphous materials such as [[Opal|opal]] and obsidian are better called mineraloids.

A compound occurring with different crystal structures yields different species: [[Quartz|quartz]] and stishovite are both silicon dioxide. Composition may vary within a species, as in mackinawite, (Fe,Ni)₉S₈, where nickel replaces some iron. Continuous series are sometimes split arbitrarily, as in the [[Olivine|olivine]] group, whose end-members forsterite and fayalite count as separate minerals. Varieties can have their own names; [[Amethyst|amethyst]] is a purple variety of quartz.

Descriptions include hardness, lustre, color, streak, cleavage, specific gravity, magnetism, fluorescence, and reaction to acid. Minerals are classified by key chemical constituents, chiefly under the Dana and Strunz systems. Groups include native elements, sulfides (galena, PbS), oxides, halides (rock salt, NaCl), carbonates (calcite, CaCO₃), sulfates (gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O), phosphates, and silicates, which make up approximately 90% of [[Earth's crust|Earth's crust]].

Extraction of valuable minerals and other geological materials from the Earth. Mining is required to obtain most materials that cannot be grown through agriculture or feasibly made artificially in a laboratory or factory. Products include metals, [[Coal|coal]], oil shale, gemstones, limestone, chalk, rock salt, potash, gravel, and clay; in a wider sense the term covers any non-renewable resource, such as petroleum, natural gas, or even water. An [[Ore|ore]] must contain a valuable constituent that can be extracted and sold for profit. Modern mining involves prospecting for ore bodies, assessing a proposed mine's profit potential, extraction, and reclamation of the land after closure. Primary methods are underground mining, surface open-pit mining, and placer mining.

The oldest known mine in the archaeological record is the Ngwenya Mine in [[Eswatini]], which radiocarbon dating indicates is about 41,000–43,000 years old; Paleolithic people mined hematite there to make the red pigment ochre. Flint mines such as Grimes Graves and Krzemionki are mostly Neolithic (c. 4000–3000 BC) and followed seams underground in chalk. Ancient Egyptians mined malachite, turquoise, copper, gypsum, granite, and gold. The gold mines of Nubia were among the most extensive, and the Greek author Diodorus Siculus mentions fire-setting as a way to break down the hard rock. The silver mines of Laurium, worked by over 20,000 slaves, helped support [[Athens]]. [[Philip II of Macedon]] captured the gold mines of Mount Pangeo in 357 BC to fund his military campaigns. The Romans developed large-scale methods, using water brought to the minehead by numerous [[Aqueduct (water supply)|aqueducts]] for removing overburden, a process called hydraulic mining.

Mining is associated with land degradation, water contamination, habitat loss, occupational health risks, and community displacement. Most nations regulate it to reduce these impacts, but governments frequently fail to enforce the rules fully, because mining often generates much of the business in rural, remote, or economically depressed communities. Unregulated, poorly regulated, or illegal mining, especially in developing economies, frequently contributes to local human rights violations and environmental conflicts. Where enforced, modern practices have significantly improved safety.

River, central United States, flowing from northern Minnesota to the [[Gulf of Mexico]]. It is the primary river of the largest drainage basin in the U.S. and the second-longest river in the country after the [[Missouri River|Missouri]]. From its traditional source at Lake Itasca, 1,475 feet (450 m) above sea level, it flows generally south for 2,340 miles (3,770 km) to the Mississippi River Delta. Its watershed drains all or parts of 32 U.S. states and two Canadian provinces; the total drainage basin is 1,151,000 square miles (2,980,000 sq km), of which only about one percent is in Canada. It ranks as the world's tenth-largest river by discharge and the largest in North America. The name comes from *Misi-ziibi* ("Great River"), the Anishinaabe ([[Ojibwe]]) name rendered by the French as *Misi zipi*.

The river is divided into the Upper Mississippi, from the headwaters to the confluence with the Missouri at St. Louis; the Middle Mississippi, from the Missouri to the Ohio; and the Lower Mississippi, from the Ohio to the Gulf. Between Lake Itasca and St. Louis, 43 dams moderate the flow, 29 of them with locks to improve commercial navigation, and thousands of wing dikes help maintain an open channel.

Native Americans have lived along the river for thousands of years; some, such as the Mound Builders, formed agricultural and urban civilizations. European exploration began in the 16th century, including the expedition of [[Hernando de Soto]] in 1541. The river formed borders for New Spain, New France, and the early United States, and the Treaty of Paris set it as the western border of the new country. After the [[Louisiana Purchase]] in 1803, it and its tributaries became pathways for westward expansion, and it became the subject of American literature, notably the writings of [[Mark Twain]]. Its final capture by Union forces in the [[American Civil War]] marked a turning point toward Union victory.

In the 20th century, massive engineering works such as [[Levee|levees]], locks, and dams were built, with a major aim of preventing the lower river from shifting into the Atchafalaya River channel and bypassing New Orleans. Agricultural runoff has produced elevated nutrient levels that are the primary contributor to the Gulf of Mexico dead zone.

Portable wireless telephone that makes and receives calls over a radio frequency link while moving within a designated service area. The link connects to the switching systems of a mobile phone operator, giving access to the public switched telephone network. Modern mobile telephony relies on a cellular network architecture, which is why the device is called a "cell phone" in North America. Digital phones support [[Text messaging|text]] and multimedia messaging, email, internet access (via LTE, 5G NR, or [[Wi-Fi]]), short-range technologies such as [[Bluetooth]], photography, video recording, gaming, streaming, satellite-based navigation and messaging, and payments by QR code or near-field communication. Phones offering only basic features are called feature phones; those with advanced computing power are [[Smartphone|smartphones]].

In 1917 the Finnish inventor Eric Tigerstedt filed a patent for a "pocket-size folding telephone with a very thin carbon microphone". The zeroth-generation (0G) services that followed World War II were not cellular, supported few simultaneous calls, and were very expensive. In 1973 John F. Mitchell and Martin Cooper of Motorola demonstrated the first handheld cellular phone, a handset weighing about 2 kg (4.4 lb); Cooper made the first call, to Joel S. Engel, a rival at [[AT&T]]. Nippon Telegraph and Telephone launched the first commercial automated cellular network, analog (1G), in [[Japan]] in 1979, and the Nordic Mobile Telephone system followed in 1981 in Denmark, Finland, Norway, and Sweden. The DynaTAC 8000x, the first commercially available handheld phone, appeared in 1983. In 1991 Radiolinja launched second-generation (2G) digital cellular technology on the GSM standard in [[Finland]]; GSM was a European initiative, and 13 European countries signed a memorandum of understanding on it in 1987.

From 1993 to 2024, worldwide subscriptions grew to over 9.1 billion, enough for one for every person on Earth. In 2024 the top smartphone manufacturers were [[Samsung]], Apple, and Xiaomi, and smartphones were about 50 percent of mobile phone sales. In the U.K., the number of phones overtook the number of houses in 1999. Studies by agencies such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and National Cancer Institute have found no causal evidence that radiofrequency radiation causes cancer beyond potential thermal effects at high exposure, but distracted use causes accidents, and critics raise concerns about data collection and electronic waste.

Current period of human history, originally applied to Europe and the West for events after classical antiquity and the Middle Ages, often from around the year 1500. Since the 1990s historians have more commonly called the period from the end of the Middle Ages to the 19th century the [[Early modern period|early modern period]], and the modern period is now more often used for events from the 19th century to the present. The time since the end of World War II (1945) can also be described as [[Contemporary history|contemporary history]]. The common definition is associated with the [[French Revolution]], the [[Industrial Revolution]], and the transition from nationalism toward the liberal international order.

Periodization is imprecise. The year 1500 is an approximate start because many major events changed the Western world around then: the fall of Constantinople (1453), Gutenberg's movable-type printing press (1450s), Christopher Columbus's voyage to the Americas (1492), and the Reformation, begun with Martin Luther's Ninety-five Theses (1517). The term "modern" was coined shortly before 1585 to describe the beginning of a new era, and the difference between "early modern" and "modern" was defined by the French and Industrial Revolutions. The European [[Renaissance]] (14th–16th centuries), which started in Italy, is an important transition period. "Modernity" and "modernism" refer to a new way of thinking distinct from medieval thinking, while "postmodernism", coined in 1949, describes a movement in art. These terms stem from European history; in China, India, and the Islamic world they are applied differently, often in the context of contact with European culture during the [[Age of Discovery]].

The early modern milestones include Niccolò Machiavelli's *The Prince* (c. 1513); Nicolaus Copernicus's *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium* (1543), proposing that the Earth revolves around the Sun; the Council of Trent (1545), beginning the Catholic Counter-Reformation; Tycho Brahe's observation of a new star (1572); Johannes Kepler's *Astronomia nova* (1609), with the first mention of elliptical planetary orbits; Galileo Galilei's *Starry Messenger* (1610), the first published work of telescopic observations; the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648); the Peace of Westphalia (1648), which established the principle of state sovereignty; Isaac Newton's *Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica* (1687), formulating the laws of motion and universal gravitation; and the Glorious Revolution (1688), which affirmed parliamentary supremacy in England.

The period has seen significant development in science, politics, warfare, and technology, and the strengthening of European, and later colonial, political, economic, and cultural dominance over the rest of the world. Starting in Western countries, it brought a systematic re-evaluation of value systems, monarchical regimes, and feudal economic systems, often replaced by democratic and liberal ideas. It is closely associated with individualism, capitalism, socialism, urbanization, and belief in the positive possibilities of technological and political progress. The world wars, the Cold War, and other conflicts have prompted reactions against modern development: [[Postmodernism|postmodernism]] has criticized the belief in constant progress, and postcolonial theory has criticized the dominance of Western Europe and North America.

Early 20th-century movement in literature, visual arts, performing arts, and music that emphasized experimentation, abstraction, and subjective experience. Philosophy, politics, architecture, and social issues were also aspects of it. It emerged during the late 19th century in response to secularization, the growing influence of science, and technological innovation, industrialization, and urbanization, and was further shaped by the cultural and geopolitical shifts after [[World War I]]. Its adherents held beliefs in a "growing alienation" from prevailing "morality, optimism, and convention".

Modernism was characterized by a self-conscious rejection of tradition and a search for new means of cultural expression, and it took a critical stance toward Enlightenment rationalism. It rejected the idea of absolute originality, *creatio ex nihilo*, upheld in the 19th century by realism and [[Romanticism]], replacing it with collage, reprise, rewriting, revision, and parody. Its reflexivity about artistic and social convention led to experimentation that highlighted how works of art are made. Associated techniques and movements include abstract art, literary stream-of-consciousness, cinematic montage, musical atonality and twelve-tone music, modern dance, modernist architecture, and urban planning; [[Cubism]] in visual art, *Ulysses* in literature, and the International Style in architecture are often cited as breakthroughs. [[Ezra Pound]]'s imperative to "make it new" is often taken as its motto, and [[W. B. Yeats]]'s line "Things fall apart; the centre cannot hold" sums up literary modernism, which often searches for a metaphysical center and experiences its collapse. Philosophically, that collapse can be traced to [[David Hume]], who argued that we never perceive one event causing another.

Historian Roger Griffin defined modernism as a broad cultural, social, or political initiative sustained by the ethos of "the temporality of the new", seeking to restore a "sense of sublime order and purpose" to a fragmenting, secularizing world. In his view, phenomena as varied as Expressionism, Futurism, psychoanalysis, eugenics, and utopian town planning share a common cause. Religion was also influenced, giving rise to Catholic modernism.

Critics have charged modernism with elitism, incomprehensibility to broad audiences, and, in built environments, a sterile inhumanity. [[Postmodernism]] rejects many of its principles and, by contrast, celebrates the collapse of metaphysics. Debate about the movement's timeline continues, with some scholars arguing that it evolved into late or high modernism.

Electrically neutral group of two or more atoms held together by attractive forces known as [[Chemical bond|chemical bonds]]. Depending on context, the term may or may not include [[Ion|ions]]; in quantum physics, organic chemistry, and biochemistry the distinction is dropped, and molecule is often used for polyatomic ions. A molecule may be homonuclear, consisting of atoms of one element, as in oxygen (O₂), or heteronuclear, a chemical compound of more than one element, as in water (H₂O). In the kinetic theory of gases, the term is used for any gaseous particle regardless of composition, which relaxes the two-atom requirement because the [[Noble gas|noble gases]] are single atoms. Atoms and complexes joined by non-covalent interactions, such as hydrogen bonds or ionic bonds, are typically not considered single molecules, and many everyday substances, such as rocks, salts, and metals, are large crystalline networks rather than discrete molecules.

In [[Covalent bond|covalent bonds]], atoms share electron pairs. The three-dimensional structure that results can be predicted by valence-shell electron-pair repulsion (VSEPR) theory, which gives methane a tetrahedral shape and water a bent one, and it influences polarity, reactivity, and interactions with other molecules. Macromolecules such as proteins and DNA are large [[Polymer|polymers]] that provide structure, catalyze reactions, and store genetic information in living organisms.

Similar concepts were discussed in antiquity, when Leucippus and Democritus argued that the universe is composed of atoms and voids. The modern concept traces to [[Robert Boyle]]'s 1661 hypothesis, in *The Sceptical Chymist*, that matter is composed of clusters of particles and that chemical change results from their rearrangement. The word *molécule* is attested in French from 1678 and became popular through discussions of the natural philosophy of René Descartes. [[Amedeo Avogadro]]'s 1811 paper held that the smallest particles of gases are not necessarily simple atoms but groups of atoms united by attraction. In 1926 Jean Perrin received the Nobel Prize in physics for proving conclusively the existence of molecules, calculating the Avogadro constant by three methods. In 1927 Fritz London and Walter Heitler applied quantum mechanics to the hydrogen molecule, bringing chemistry under quantum mechanics, and their work influenced [[Linus Pauling]], who published his ground-breaking work on the chemical bond in 1931.

Phylum of invertebrate animals including snails, slugs, clams, oysters, squid, cuttlefish, and octopuses; its members are called molluscs or mollusks. Some 89,857 extant species are recognized, with estimates ranging over 251,000, making it the second-largest animal phylum after [[Arthropod|Arthropoda]]. Molluscs are the largest marine phylum, about 23% of all named marine organisms, and include many freshwater and terrestrial species. The phylum is typically divided into 7 or 8 classes, two entirely extinct. [[Gastropod|Gastropods]] (snails, slugs, and abalone) account for 80% of classified species. [[Cephalopod|Cephalopods]] are among the most neurologically advanced invertebrates, and either the [[Giant squid|giant squid]] or the [[Colossal squid|colossal squid]] is the largest known extant invertebrate.

The four most universal features are a soft body composed almost entirely of muscle, a mantle with a cavity used for breathing and excretion, a radula, or rasping "tongue" (absent in bivalves), and the structure of the nervous system. The hypothetical ancestral mollusc has a single limpet-like shell of proteins and chitin reinforced with calcium carbonate, secreted by the mantle, and a muscular foot beneath. Circulation is mainly open. Most molluscs have eyes, and nearly all produce eggs, from which trochophore or veliger larvae or miniature adults emerge. Evidence for gastropods, cephalopods, and bivalves appears in the [[Cambrian]], 541–485.4 million years ago, but their evolutionary history remains debated.

Molluscs have long been a food source, though toxins can accumulate in some and cause food poisoning. They have yielded luxury goods, notably [[Pearl|pearls]], mother of pearl, Tyrian purple dye, and sea silk, and their shells served as money in some preindustrial societies. The bite of the [[Blue-ringed octopus|blue-ringed octopus]] is often fatal, and stings from some large tropical cone shells can kill, though their venoms have become tools in neurological research. Schistosomiasis, transmitted by water snails, affects about 200 million people. Snails and slugs can be serious agricultural pests, and some introduced species have seriously damaged ecosystems.

The name derives from the French *mollusque* and post-classical Latin *mollis*, "soft", and was used in taxonomy by J. Jonston in 1650. The study of molluscs is called malacology.

Hereditary form of government in which political power is legally passed to family members of the monarch, a head of state who rules for life, or a polity with this form of government. Monarchs may be entirely ceremonial, hold executive powers, or have absolute power, and they may also gain authority through election. There are conventionally two types: [[Absolute monarchy]], governed as autocracy, and [[Constitutional monarchy]], in which a constitution leaves the monarch legal and ceremonial roles with limited or no political power. Most modern monarchies are constitutional. The word comes from the Greek *monarkhia*, "absolute rule", from *monos* ("alone") and *arkhein* ("to rule").

Chiefdoms, or tribal kingship, are prehistoric and provided the concept of state formation. Among the oldest recorded monarchies were those of [[Narmer]], pharaoh of Egypt c. 3100 BC, and Enmebaragesi, Sumerian king of Kish c. 2600 BC. In several ancient cultures the monarch held sacral functions connected to sacrifice and was sometimes identified with divine ancestry, possibly establishing the notion of the divine right of kings. Polybius identified monarchy as one of three "benign" forms of government, with aristocracy and democracy. In antiquity some monarchies were abolished in favor of assemblies, as in the [[Roman Republic]] (509 BC). By the 17th century monarchy was challenged by evolving parliamentarism and by anti-monarchism, including the temporary overthrow of the English monarchy by Parliament in 1649, the [[American Revolution]] of 1776, and the [[French Revolution]] of 1789. Advocacy of abolition is called republicanism, and advocacy of monarchy monarchism. In 1848 a wave of revolutions abolished many monarchies.

Nearly half of independent states at the start of the 19th century were monarchies. The proportion peaked in the middle of that century and has steadily declined, with republics replacing many monarchies, notably at the end of [[World War I]] and World War II. Today 43 sovereign nations have a monarch, including fifteen Commonwealth realms that have [[Charles III]] as head of state. Some retain real power: in Morocco, Qatar, Liechtenstein, and Thailand, the hereditary monarch has more political influence than any other single source of authority, and Saudi Arabia is an absolute monarchy. Some analyses report stronger economic growth in constitutional monarchies than in republics, though reverse causality has been proposed.
